answer: Two problem statements: (1) a word dictionary without any database, and (2) a superfast key-value store. Both chosen to build foundational blocks; both are used in production (the second is revealed as Bitcask).
evidence: Overview: 'The agenda is two problem statements: a word dictionary without any database, and a superfast key-value store.'

answer: Ruled out: every traditional/off-the-shelf database - MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcache, nothing; the data must live in plain files. Relaxed: performance - a high response time is acceptable (caching/batching etc. covered elsewhere). Demanded: portability - literally one file holding everything needed to read/write it, copy and ship it.
evidence: Ch1.1: 'no MySQL, no Postgres, no MongoDB, no Redis, no Elasticsearch, no Memcache, nothing'; 'Performance is not today's problem. A high response time is acceptable'; 'What is required is portability.'

answer: No live, pointed updates. Once a week (say every Sunday) a changelog file arrives by email holding only the words that changed and their new meanings, and it is applied to whatever store you built. One huge processing pass a week is acceptable.
evidence: Ch1.1: 'There are no live, pointed updates. Once a week, say every Sunday, a changelog file arrives by email holding only the words that changed and their new meanings'

answer: Lookup is always a single word: given a word return its meaning, else 404; no autocomplete. It is a key-value store: key = word, value = a two- or three-line meaning. Sizes: whole dictionary 1 TB, 170,000 words (several MB per word - on purpose, imagine multimedia baked in).
evidence: Ch1.1: 'A lookup is always a single word. There is no autocomplete... if the word does not exist, return 404. The whole dictionary is 1 TB, and it holds 170,000 words.'

answer: Storage, query, portability, and seamless updates.
evidence: Ch1.1: 'Every design that follows is judged on four axes: storage, query, portability and seamless updates.'

answer: Querying JSON means unmarshalling it, which is very expensive; to check whether one word exists you must read the entire JSON file, deserialize it, build an in-memory object (e.g. hash map) and only then check - at 1 TB really costly, and the format gives no direct way to reach one entry. (JSON Lines streams record by record but still has no index, so still a scan.)
evidence: Ch1.2: 'Querying JSON means unmarshalling it, which is a very expensive process'; 'to check whether one word exists, you read the entire JSON file, deserialize it, build an in-memory object...'

answer: A CSV-like plain text file, one line per word: the word, a comma, its meaning, then newline - e.g. 'apple,a fruit' newline 'amazon,a rainforest', 1 TB in all. (A write-ahead-log style format was suggested but not taken up.)
evidence: Ch1.2: 'It is CSV-like, one line per word: apple,a fruit, a newline, then amazon and its meaning'

answer: The dictionary must not contain the same word twice - no repetitive entries (so an update can't simply be written as another line). Why: there are no columns, only words and meanings; imagine the file opened in a text editor with repeats in it - a portable file can't carry duplicates.
evidence: Ch1.2: 'the dictionary must not contain the same word twice... remember that a portable file can't carry duplicates. That becomes a requirement of its own: no repetitive entries.'

answer: No - response time isn't a constraint, so sorting brings nothing yet; words can sit in any order. Accepted for starters; sorting returns in 5.3 when the weekly update (merge) needs it.
evidence: Ch1.2: 'The first answer was no: response time isn't a constraint, so sorting brings nothing yet... For starters, that is accepted.'

answer: Very read-heavy: a thousand reads to one write would understate it; the real ratio is much more skewed (>> 1000:1).
evidence: Ch1.1: 'a thousand reads to one write would understate it, and the real ratio is much more skewed than that.' Fig 1a: 'read-heavy: >> 1000 : 1'

answer: Agreed a single-word update cannot be very costly (shouldn't 'boil the ocean' with heavy IO or a scan of every file for one change), but since updates arrive as one weekly batch, one huge processing pass a week is acceptable.
evidence: Ch1.1: 'A single-word update indeed cannot be very costly. But updates arrive as one weekly batch, so one huge processing pass a week is acceptable.'

answer: Multiple files kill portability (must be literally one file). A single zip of many folders: you would still have to extract it to use it; it is still many logical files, often compressed, so there is no direct byte-offset read into the dictionary's data.
evidence: Ch1.3: 'Rejected: with multiple files you kill portability.'; zip 'Rejected: you would still have to extract it... no direct byte-offset read'

answer: AWS Athena - uploading a plain CSV to S3 and querying it seamlessly (in the lecture's telling Athena keeps an index handy with the file). Page notes Athena actually scans files and bills per TB scanned; the dictionary shares only the idea of querying plain files on S3 without a DB server. Kept simple because not many people know Parquet/Avro, and the aim is to keep it really simple - the points behind them are used, just not through Parquet; Lucene's good parts kept one level down: simple version first, then next level.
evidence: Ch1.3 'What this simulates': 'a service called Athena'; Parquet: 'Not many people know these formats, and the aim is to keep it really simple'; Lucene: 'the simple version first, then the next level.'

answer: It's over-engineering for a very simple dictionary: no B+ trees, nothing fancy; and why only 1,000 keys in memory - far more fit. Keep it very simple, that's where you see the power and beauty of the system. Start naive. (Page: page-based B+ trees matter when the index is too big for RAM, not the case here; the offset idea survives.)
evidence: Ch2.1: 'And why only 1,000 keys in memory? Far more fit. For a very simple word dictionary all of this is over-engineering: no B+ trees, nothing fancy.'

answer: Store as CSV text file; open file, read line by line until the key is found, stop, read the meaning, return. Cost: worst case reads the whole 1 TB; on average half, 0.5 TB = 500 GB per request, paid again on every request.
evidence: Ch2.1: 'In the worst case every request reads the whole 1 TB file; on average it reads half of it, 0.5 TB, which is 500 GB per request.'

answer: It degrades the disk's performance and wears the disk out - sectors go bad from heavy overuse; it is a hardware, software and time problem at once (wastes throughput, pushes drives past rated workload, reducing reliability).
evidence: Ch2.1: 'degrades the disk's performance, and wears the disk out: its sectors go bad... a hardware problem, a software problem and a time problem at once.'

answer: Indexing - and then do the number crunch: how big will the index be, does it fit in memory?
evidence: Ch2.1 rule: 'Whenever reads are slow, the only thing that should come to your mind is indexing.'

answer: Each entry: the key (word) and its offset in the data file. The offset is the byte position where the word's line starts - the nth byte from the beginning of the file, a count of bytes, not a line number (e.g. apple 0, amazon 14, book 34).
evidence: Ch2.2: 'Each index entry holds two things: the key and its offset... the nth byte from the beginning of the file. It is a count of bytes, not a line number.'

answer: The index holds only keys and small offsets, so you don't iterate over megabytes of meanings; the small index file is very fast to read sequentially even in the worst case (a couple of MB vs a terabyte). Then one pointed read of one line.
evidence: Ch2.2: 'The index holds only keys and small offsets... you are not iterating over megabytes of meanings, and the small index file is very fast to read sequentially, even in the worst case.'

answer: You'd still have to go through every word under that letter to find the one you want, while a per-word offset takes you straight to its line; and the full per-word index fits in memory anyway (~1.75 MB), so splitting by letter buys nothing.
evidence: Ch2.3: 'you would still have to go through every word under that letter... the full per-word index fits in memory anyway, so splitting it by letter buys nothing.'

answer: Entry size = key length + offset length + 2 (comma and newline): avg word 4.3 chars (instructor computed from a downloaded dictionary, 'not more than five') + 4-byte integer offset + 2 = 10.3 bytes; total = 170,000 x 10.3 B. (Page notes: across distinct words avg is ~7.6; and a 1 TB file needs 8-byte offsets -> 14.3 B.)
evidence: Ch2.3: 'So an entry is about 4.3 + 4 + 2 = 10.3 bytes.'; 'The offset is an integer, and an integer takes 4 bytes.'

answer: 170,000 x 10.3 B = 1,751,000 B ~ 1.75 MB (with correct 8-byte offsets ~2.4 MB). Conclusion: fits in RAM very easily, 'peanuts' next to 1 TB - load it into an in-memory hash map at server start; every lookup becomes one pointed read; settles storage and query axes.
evidence: Ch2.3: '170,000 x 10.3 B = 1,751,000 B... about 1.75 MB'; 'An index of 1.75 MB fits in RAM very easily. Next to a 1 TB data file it is peanuts.'

answer: Number crunching matters when designing any system: what looked huge (1 TB, 170,000 words) needs an index under two megabytes; one simple calculation, not a cleverer structure, settled the design - one level of indexing instead of over-complicating. Also don't take MB lightly.
evidence: Ch2.3: 'This is why number crunching matters when you design any system.'; 'One simple number crunch made the system much better: instead of over-complicating things, one level of indexing.'

answer: Index stored on disk, loaded into an in-memory hash map at API server start. A request checks the map for the word, gets the offset, goes to the data file, reads the line at that offset and returns the meaning (missing word -> 404).
evidence: Ch2.3: 'A request checks the map for the word, gets the offset, goes to the data file, reads the line at that offset and returns the meaning.'

answer: index.dict (couple of MB of words and offsets) and data.dict (the terabyte of meanings). Two files break portability: anyone copying must copy both and keep them together; portable meant literally one file.
evidence: Ch3 intro / 3.1: 'Two files, an index and a data.dictionary, break portability. Anyone who copies the dictionary has to copy both and keep them together'

answer: Every startup would iterate through the entire terabyte of data just to rebuild something that hasn't changed; the file changes only once a week, so the work is avoidable. Store the index.
evidence: Ch3.1: 'every startup then iterates through the entire terabyte of data just to rebuild something that hasn't changed. The file changes once a week, so the work is avoidable.'

answer: How does the reader know where the index ends and the data begins? (Otherwise reading line by line it carries on into data, e.g. 'apple,a fruit' read as an entry and apple's offset replaced by 'a fruit'.) First two options: a special separator line/marker between index and data; and pre-allocating a fixed-size region (first 2 MB is the index).
evidence: Ch3.1 / Fig 3a: '- special line / separator · - pre-allocate / fixed size · 2 MB'

answer: 'A very nice hack': reader knows the first 2 MB are index without looking (a little more than today's 1.751 MB since few words get added weekly), but it wastes a little space, and the push was to be more frugal.
evidence: Ch3.1: '"A very nice hack", in the lecture's words, though it wastes a little space, and the push was to be more frugal.'

answer: It still leaves the original problem: when the two meet, how do you know where one finished and the other begins? The gap is unused space until then, and the fallback was again a separator.
evidence: Ch3.1: 'on the day the two meet, how do you know where one finished and the other begins? The gap between them is unused space until then, and the fallback, once more, was a separator.'

answer: Store the boundary as a number - the byte offset / index size - directly at the start of the file in a small fixed-size chunk, removing the separator. General name: a (fixed-size) file header - the classic mechanism of file formats (PNG, JPG, MP3, AVI): first bytes hold meta information about the rest.
evidence: Ch3.2: 'store the byte offset directly at the start of the file... That first chunk is a header, and it is the classic mechanism of file formats everywhere'

answer: 1) Name/magic 'OUR_DICT' - 8 bytes; 2) version - 4 bytes; 3) index size - 4 bytes. Total 16 bytes, fixed width.
evidence: Ch3.2: 'a fixed-width header of 16 bytes: 8 for the name, 4 for the version, 4 for the index size.'

answer: Magic name tells the decoder 'this is our dictionary' and lets it recognise the file (like PNG's 8-byte signature; your own DB would start with e.g. AODB). Version: one format can have variants (v1 index then data, v2 data then index); the decoder reads the version and acts accordingly. (It describes the file's format/layout variant, not the data.)
evidence: Ch3.2: 'a name that tells the decoder "this is our dictionary"'; 'a version, because one format can have variants... The decoder reads the version and acts accordingly.'

answer: 1. Read the first 16 bytes (header). 2. First 8 bytes say OUR_DICT - our dictionary. 3. Next 4 bytes give the version; decoder acts on it. 4. Next 4 bytes give the index size (e.g. 1,751,000); read exactly that many bytes. 5. Build the in-memory hash table from the index (apple->0, amazon->14...). 6. Everything after the index is data, which the offsets point into; server ready.
evidence: Ch3.2 Fig 3c steps 1-6.

answer: Like other formats built from sections: in an MP4 the header says where the video part is and where the audio part is - video holding its frames, audio its waveform info - same header+compartments idea. (Page note: MP4 muxers usually write the moov index at the end, with 'faststart' moving it to the beginning.)
evidence: Ch3.3: 'in an MP4, the header says where the video part is and where the audio part is'; 3.2 note on moov/faststart.

answer: JSON has no header - it's a simple text file, so to get any information you read the entire file and let the decoder parse braces, quotes and strings into an in-memory dictionary first. Parquet has headers/information locating its parts - strictly a footer: PAR1, column chunks, file metadata + 4-byte length, PAR1; reader reads the footer first to find just the column chunks it needs.
evidence: Ch3.3: 'JSON has no header... you read the entire file'; 'Parquet... keeps that information in a footer... a reader reads the footer first to find the column chunks it needs'

answer: Encoder creates a file in that specific format; decoder decodes/reads it (image, video, audio, any format). evidence: Ch3.3: 'The encoder creates a file in that specific format; the decoder decodes it.'; 'It means the browser has no decoder for that format'

answer: [Header 16 B: OUR_DICT (8 B, bytes 0-7) | version (4 B, 8-11) | index size (4 B, 12-15)] [Index: word,offset entries, index_size bytes] [Data: word,meaning lines, offsets point here].
evidence: Ch3.2 Fig 3b and struct dict_header: 'then: index[index_size] word,offset lines; then: data ... word,meaning lines'

answer: Support put, get, update and delete, super fast, with full persistence (each put flushed to disk immediately), on very commodity hardware: cheap magnetic hard disks.
evidence: Ch7.1: 'Design a super fast key-value store on very commodity hardware: cheap magnetic hard disks. It must support put, get, update and delete, with full persistence.'

answer: Hierarchy CPU caches -> memory -> SSD -> magnetic disks -> tape. SSDs sit closer to memory than HDDs in both speed and cost (faster, costlier); HDDs slower, cheaper. Huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disks, not SSDs, because SSDs are very costly.
evidence: Ch7.1: 'SSDs sit closer to memory than magnetic hard disks do, both in speed and in cost... huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disks'

answer: The byte offset is translated to a physical place (disk, sector, offset in sector); the disk rotates and the magnetic head physically moves to that location, reads, sends it to the device driver, then up to user space. The mechanical movement - moving the head and rotating the disk - is the most time-consuming part.
evidence: Ch7.1: 'That mechanical movement, moving the head and rotating the disk, is the most time-consuming part of disk I/O.'

answer: That every put must be persisted to disk immediately (flushed) - so a memtable buffering writes in memory doesn't fit.
evidence: Ch7.2: 'That doesn't fit the requirement as set: every put must be persisted to disk immediately.'

answer: Every put is appended at the end of one file (a write-ahead-style log/ledger), flushed (fsync) before ack. Best on magnetic disk because the head is already where the last write ended: no seek, no waiting for the platter to spin round - zero seek, no big mechanical movement.
evidence: Ch7.2: 'Append only, zero seek, no big mechanical movement: the best you can do.'

answer: K1 V1' is appended at the end (O4) like any other entry; the old K1 V1 isn't touched and simply becomes obsolete (map repointed from O1 to O4).
evidence: Ch7.2: 'The new entry is appended like any other, and the old one simply becomes obsolete.'

answer: Because it's an append-only file: you cannot write to any location other than the end (random reads yes, random writes no).
evidence: Ch7.3: 'But this is an append-only file: you cannot write to any other location.'

answer: As a put with a special marker value: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1), appended at end; K2 removed from the in-memory map. Gives O(1) delete, as efficient as put; dead entries cleaned later in merge.
evidence: Ch7.3: 'Delete is a put with a special value, DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1).'; 'a delete implemented as a put is just as efficient.'

answer: Naive: start at the top, look at every entry, return the latest for the key - very poor. Fast: in-memory hash table mapping each key to the offset of its latest entry (offset, not value), updated on each append; get goes straight to the offset - one memory lookup, one disk read.
evidence: Ch7.4: 'Keep an in-memory hash table that maps each key to the offset of its latest entry in the file'

answer: Allows reading anywhere in what was written (random reads); forbids writing anywhere before the end (no random writes).
evidence: Ch7.3: 'Random reads, yes; random writes, no.'

answer: Each op: append to disk first, note offset, then update map. PUT K1 V1 at O1 -> K1->O1; PUT K2 V2 at O2 -> K2->O2; PUT K3 V3 at O3 -> K3->O3; PUT K1 V1' at O4 -> K1 repointed to O4; DEL K2 appends K2 -1 at O5 and removes K2 from map. Final: K1->O4, K3->O3, no K2.
evidence: Ch7.4 clip text and Fig 7c.

answer: GET: look up key in map; no entry -> 404 (no disk read); entry -> read at that offset, return value. After crash: map gone but file safe on disk; on restart read the whole file from the top and rebuild the map (later entries win, -1 removes key); takes a long time, accepted in this design (can't answer until done).
evidence: Ch7.4: 'on restart you go through the entire file and rebuild the index. That can take a long time, and for this design that is accepted.'

answer: Every key (not values) must fit in memory, so the number of keys is bounded by RAM. (Also slow restart to rebuild it.)
evidence: Ch8.1: 'every key has to fit in memory... So you can store only as many keys as you can keep in RAM.'

answer: It never collects anything, so it grows huge and the system eventually runs out of disk space. Against one/few huge files: a single huge file can't be indexed concurrently (smaller pieces can); cleaning smaller pieces is more even; biggest reason (per teacher): the file system may not support files over a terabyte (BTRFS, NTFS limits). Page caveat: modern FSs allow many TB (FAT32 caps 4 GB); stronger reason is merge/compaction/index rebuild work file by file.
evidence: Ch8.1 third weakness; 8.2: 'The biggest reason of all is the file system.'

answer: Keep smaller files - say 100 MB or 1 GB - and rotate: when the active file crosses that threshold, start writing a new one (real Bitcask: 2 GB default max_file_size).
evidence: Ch8.2: 'keep smaller files: say 100 MB, or 1 GB. As soon as the active file crosses that threshold, start writing to a new one.'

answer: Exactly one active file takes all writes; the others are read-only/immutable but still readable - a get goes to whichever file holds its key (active or older). The map must store which file and which offset per key (K1 -> f1, O4).
evidence: Ch8.2: 'At any point in time exactly one file is active, and all writes go to it. Every other file is read-only, but it can still be read.'; 'it has to say which file the key is in, and at which offset'

answer: A separate process (while the active file takes writes) iterates the read-only files and writes one new file combining them, without stale or deleted entries; old files are then deleted forever. Afterwards the in-memory map must be updated for every entry that moved (new file, new offsets) - atomically, per the prepared notes.
evidence: Ch8.3: 'the in-memory map must be updated for every entry that moved into the new file. The prepared notes add one word: update it atomically.'

answer: A sawtooth: usage climbs with writes, drops suddenly at each merge and compaction. Bounded by the disk's maximum capacity (e.g. 1 TB cap line); crossing it crashes the system.
evidence: Ch8.4: 'You will see this sawtooth pattern'; 'If the disk is 1 TB, you cannot let usage grow beyond 1 TB.'

answer: 1) Merge and compaction frequency; 2) file rotation threshold (how big a file may grow). Tune by monitoring the sawtooth while building the store, then decide; expose both as configurable parameters. Merge too often: too much garbage collection, CPU not free for real work. Too rarely: work piles up, a peak hits the disk cap and the store crashes.
evidence: Ch8.4: 'So this design has two configurable parameters...'; 'Merge too often... Merge too rarely and a lot of work piles up.'

answer: You still get benefits but not as significant, since SSDs don't use a rotating disk; flash handles writes well. (Page: flash can't overwrite in place, so append-only stays flash-friendly; zoned SSDs require sequential writes.)
evidence: Ch8.4: 'On SSDs you still get benefits, but not as significant, because SSDs don't use a rotating disk'

answer: Files are read by blocks, not lines; reading one byte at a time until newline means one disk I/O (read call) per byte - very slow ('school kid' code). (Page: page cache means most don't reach disk, but still slow.)
evidence: Ch9.1: 'if you read one byte at a time until you hit \n, you make one disk I/O per byte, and that makes things very slow.'

answer: Put key size and value size before the key and value, each a 4-byte integer (8 bytes total). Read: first I/O reads the 8 bytes (KSZ, VSZ); add them; second I/O reads exactly that many bytes, split into key and value - two disk I/Os, read predictability (same idea as dictionary header).
evidence: Ch9.1: 'Each is a 4-byte integer, 8 bytes together... Reading a record is now two disk I/Os.'

answer: Machine crashes/power goes halfway through writing a gigantic value ('written 110 then the power went'): entry corrupt, can't fix it, but must know it lost integrity and not serve it. Dangerous because after restart the next entry is appended right after; reading 'value size' bytes from the broken entry runs into the next entry -> garbage.
evidence: Ch9.2: 'A partial entry is dangerous for a second reason... the read runs into the entry after it.'

answer: CRC = cyclic redundancy check, a checksum: simple hash over everything in the record - key size, value size, key, value - computed in memory and stored with it. Placed leftmost because it's the first thing written and made sure is flushed - the bare minimum to know something is corrupt (same instinct as ID generators putting timestamp leftmost); network formats too. Examples cited in class: Postgres commit log and MySQL binlog put CRC leftmost. Page correction: Postgres WAL has it at end of record header, MySQL in last 4 bytes of event; Bitcask and LevelDB put it first.
evidence: Ch9.2: 'Good persistent record formats do this: the Postgres commit log puts the CRC on the leftmost side, and so does the MySQL binlog.' + More precisely note.

answer: CRC | TS (timestamp) | KSZ (key size) | VSZ (value size) | K | V. TS is just for conflicts.
evidence: Ch9.2: 'So the final record is: CRC, timestamp (just for conflicts), key size, value size, key, value.'

answer: Writes in order: header part, then key, then the large value. If the first write fails, the entry doesn't exist. If a later write fails, on read the CRC doesn't match -> tell the user the entry is corrupted, never serve it. Recovery is heuristic: ignore that entry in merge and compaction (and elsewhere), assume the write never came - corrupt data can't be recovered.
evidence: Ch9.2: 'You ignore that entry, in merge and compaction and elsewhere, and assume the write never came your way'

answer: Per key: file (id), entry size, offset, and timestamp (for conflicts/meta). GET: 1) hash table lookup, 2) disk seek, 3) disk read.
evidence: Ch10.1: 'it stores the file the key is in, the size of the record, the offset, and a timestamp'; Fig 10a '1 hash table lookup · 2 disk seek · 3 disk read'

answer: Bitcask's entries aren't sorted (write order), so it's not a merge-sort two-pointer merge; instead load entries into a temporary hash table (later entry replaces, delete removes) and flush it. The dictionary merge worked with two pointers because both files were sorted.
evidence: Ch8.3: 'It is not like the merge step of merge sort, because these entries are not sorted'
